title: Summer and Vow
premise: Paloma Brightwater has spent ten years writing letters to an anonymous correspondent whose words once pulled her out of grief after her grandfather's death — letters she answered but never signed, believing the exchange ended long ago. When a quiet stranger named Jonah Vane rents the cottage beside her lighthouse on the Cornish coast, she discovers he is the letter-writer, dying of a degenerative illness and come to find her before his memory fails completely. As they fall into a love neither planned, Paloma must weigh the literary career built on the novel she wrote from their letters against a future with a man who is already forgetting her. In the end she chooses him: she gives up her publisher's deadline, and in the book's final scene, when Jonah no longer remembers their decade of correspondence, she reads their letters aloud to him each evening by the lamp — beginning again, every day, choosing love over legacy.
about_author: Edmund Amberdale is the pen name of a former lighthouse archivist who spent seven years cataloguing correspondence salvaged from coastal stations along the English seaboard. Summer and Vow is a second novel inspired by an unsigned bundle of letters found sealed in a keeper's logbook.

chapters.title: The Lamp Room
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She tends her late grandfather's automated lighthouse out of ritual rather than duty, drafting chapters of her debut novel between shifts. Establishes her guarded heart and her habit of keeping love 'in the past tense.' Emotional beat: comfortable loneliness about to be disturbed.

chapters.title: A Tenant at Gull Cottage
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A reserved newcomer, Jonah Vane, rents the neighboring cottage for the summer, asking odd questions about the lighthouse's history. Their first meeting is prickly; he seems to study her more than the scenery. Beat: unease flickering beneath polite small talk.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Ink
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, flashback woven through present. We learn of the anonymous correspondent who wrote to her after her grandfather's drowning — letters that saved her — and how the exchange stopped without explanation. Beat: grief reframed as gratitude, and an old wound reopened by Jonah's arrival.

chapters.title: Salt and Small Talk
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He watches Paloma from his window, rehearsing confessions he cannot make, hiding tremors in his hands that hint at something wrong. A storm forces them to share shelter in the boathouse. Beat: longing constrained by a secret and a ticking clock.

chapters.title: The Manuscript Offer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Her London publisher accepts her novel — built secretly on the letters — with a lucrative contract and a brutal deadline. Celebration feels strangely hollow. Beat: triumph shadowed by guilt over profiting from someone else's words.

chapters.title: What the Tide Brought In
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Walking the shore, Jonah loses time — minutes gone, a path forgotten — and hides a neurologist's letter deeper in his coat. He nearly tells Paloma; instead he asks about her novel. Beat: fear hardening into resolve to reach her before memory abandons him.

chapters.title: Chapters Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She reads her draft aloud on the headland; Jonah recognizes phrases unmistakably lifted from his own letters and realizes she never knew who he was. He says nothing. Beat: wonder curdling into heartbreak — she loved his words without knowing him.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Logbook
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Sorting her grandfather's effects, she finds a bundle of unsent drafts in his handwriting — proof he was her correspondent all along, and that he died before sending the last one. Beat: devastation, and the collapse of the story she told herself for a decade.

chapters.title: An Honest Evening
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Over fish and chips and cheap wine, Jonah and Paloma trade truths — hers about the manuscript, his only half-truths about why he came. The intimacy terrifies them both. Beat: two people falling in love while withholding the one fact that matters most.

chapters.title: Deadline
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Her editor demands revisions and a publicity tour; the novel's success would expose the letters publicly. Paloma hesitates for the first time in her ambitious life. Beat: duty versus conscience, the career that saved everything now demanding a price.

chapters.title: The Diagnosis in the Drawer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Searching Jonah's cottage for a borrowed corkscrew, she finds the neurologist's letter: early-onset dementia, progressive, irreversible. She flees before he sees her. Beat: shock, betrayal-adjacent anger, and the terrible arithmetic of falling for a disappearing man.

chapters.title: Confrontation at Low Water
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. On the exposed tidal flats, Paloma demands the truth; Jonah admits everything — the illness, the move, and finally that he was not the writer: he was the one who delivered his dying father's letters, then continued them himself out of love begun secondhand. Beat: fury giving way to a more complicated tenderness.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She rereads every letter with new eyes and recognizes Jonah's voice in the later ones — steadier, funnier, more afraid. She understands he has loved her for years without permission. Beat: the past tense collapses into the present.

chapters.title: First Light
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. They become lovers quietly, stealing mornings before the village wakes. But Jonah forgets a promise within hours of making it, and pretends otherwise. Beat: happiness braided with dread; love learning to live inside a shrinking window.

chapters.title: The Publisher's Gambit
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Her editor proposes marketing the novel around its 'true story' and hunting down the mysterious correspondent. Paloma refuses and threatens to walk away from the contract entirely. Beat: the career that saved everything now poised to destroy the person who matters.

chapters.title: Vow at the Lighthouse
chapters.summary: Both POVs converging. At the top of the tower at dusk, Jonah asks nothing except that she remember for both of them; Paloma answers with a private vow — not marriage, but presence. Beat: the emotional summit; love chosen explicitly against every prudent alternative.

chapters.title: The Missing Day
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Jonah disappears for a day, having forgotten where he was going; she finds him miles away, frightened and dignified, insisting he walked there on purpose. Beat: the illness stops being abstract; grief arrives early, while he is still here.

chapters.title: What the Novel Owes
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She rewrites the entire manuscript to tell the truth — names changed, but the love named plainly — and sends it against her agent's advice. Beat: reclamation; art realigned with honor instead of ambition.

chapters.title: Winter Comes Early
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. His decline accelerates; he begins losing whole days and sometimes mistakes Paloma for a kind stranger. He tries to push her away to spare her. Beat: the darkest hour — love against duty inverted, as he chooses self-sacrifice and she refuses it.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud, Every Evening
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She moves into Gull Cottage and establishes a ritual: each evening she reads their letters to Jonah, so that even if he remembers nothing else, he falls asleep inside their story daily. Beat: fierce, practical devotion; love as maintenance, not miracle.

chapters.title: Summer and Vow
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The rewritten novel publishes modestly; Paloma declines the tour. One morning Jonah, lucid for a rare bright interval, tells her he knows exactly who she is — 'the ending of my favorite book.' Beat: grace, brief and complete.

chapters.title: The Keeper of Both
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, coda. Years soften the loss; Jonah lives longer than predicted, and even after his death she keeps reading the letters aloud to the empty chair, then to visiting children. The lighthouse still turns. Final beat: inheritance transformed — memory kept alive by choice, love outlasting the mind that held it.
